e.t: This word means “to fight” or “to struggle.” It describes exerting oneself in a serious contest or effort, whether the struggle is against opposition or involves disciplined perseverance. In the New Testament, it is used eight times in eight verses, showing a repeated picture of determined effort rather than casual action. Its meaning can apply to physical conflict, athletic striving, or earnest labor, while the surrounding verse determines the particular setting. The word appears in passages from Luke, John, 1 Corinthians, Colossians, 1 Timothy, and 2 Timothy.

This word means “blameless”: free from blame, fault, or accusation. It describes someone or something regarded as without a valid charge against it. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times and is consistently rendered “blameless.” Its use can describe people who live without a chargeable fault, while the surrounding verse determines the precise application. The word therefore points to a condition of being beyond legitimate blame, not merely to a reputation formed by human opinion.

e.t: This word means “promptly” or “without objection.” It describes an action carried out readily, without resistance, protest, or delay. As an adverb, it tells how someone responds or acts rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 10:29. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is willing and immediate action rather than hesitation or dispute.

This word means “indecency” or an “indecent act”—conduct recognized as shameful or improper. It refers to behavior rather than merely an inward thought, and its meaning can describe an act that violates what is considered fitting or honorable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans and Revelation. The surrounding verse and passage determine the specific action or warning intended in each occurrence.

This word means “deep,” describing something that extends far downward or inward. It can refer to physical depth, such as the depth of water, and can also describe something profound or difficult to reach. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, with the same central idea of depth. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding context.

This word means “little scroll,” referring to a small written scroll or document. It is a noun, naming the physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Revelation 10:2, 10:9, and 10:10. The repeated use of the same word in this short passage keeps attention on the identity of this small scroll, while the surrounding verse text supplies its particular significance.

This word means “demons,” referring to more than one demon. It is a plural term used as a name for these beings rather than as a description of a human person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 8:31. Its basic meaning identifies the beings being discussed, while the surrounding verse and passage determine what is being said about them there.

This word means a thought—an idea or consideration held in the mind. It refers to inward thinking rather than an outward action or spoken statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 11:17. The word’s basic sense can therefore be stated simply: a thought or mental consideration. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual sentence where it appears.

This word means “approved by testing” or “tested,” describing something or someone shown to be genuine, reliable, or acceptable after examination. It points to approval that has been demonstrated rather than merely claimed. In the New Testament, it is used for people and conduct that withstand evaluation and receive commendation. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages concerned with being approved before God or recognized as faithful by others.

This word means “banquet,” referring to a prepared and generally formal meal shared by invited guests. It is a noun that names the meal itself rather than the act of inviting, eating, or celebrating. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke, where its broader meaning is understood from the surrounding passage. The word therefore points to an arranged gathering centered on food and fellowship, while the particular purpose or character of the banquet depends on its context.

e.t: This word means “be warped” or “to be warped.” It describes something that has become bent away from its proper shape or condition, emphasizing a resulting state rather than merely the act of changing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 3:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains being warped or distorted.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to look,” “to look into,” or “to look upon.” It describes directing one’s eyes toward someone or something, often with focused attention. As a verb, it expresses the act of looking rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in the Gospels, Acts, and other New Testament passages. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains purposeful looking or observing.

This word means “vomit,” referring to material expelled from the stomach. It is a concrete noun rather than a description of an action or a moral quality. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains the bodily substance brought up and expelled.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word describes being cheerful or keeping up one’s courage. It points to an inward condition of good spirits and steady confidence rather than discouragement. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing twice in Acts and once in James. Its meaning can therefore describe emotional encouragement in difficult circumstances as well as a cheerful disposition. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on maintaining courage or expressing gladness.

Eutychus is a personal name, meaning the individual called Eutychus rather than a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek New Testament, this name occurs once, in Acts 20:9. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to identify a particular person in that passage, not to express a doctrine or broader category. The name is rendered consistently as “Eutychus.”

Thaddaeus is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times identifying Thaddaeus among Jesus’ apostles. The name is rendered “Thaddaeus” in both Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18. Because it functions as a person’s name, its basic meaning is identification: it distinguishes this apostle from the other people named in those lists.

This word means “harvester” or “reaper”: a person who gathers a crop when it is ready. It names the worker responsible for cutting or collecting what has grown, rather than the crop itself or the field. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew 13, where its basic meaning identifies those who carry out the harvest. The surrounding passage determines the particular significance of that harvest, but the word itself refers plainly to the person doing the gathering.

This word means “to get acquainted” or “to get acquainted with” someone. It describes becoming familiar with a person through meeting or personal contact, rather than merely hearing about them. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Galatians 1:18. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is personal acquaintance or familiarity. It functions as an action word describing the act of coming to know someone personally.

This Greek New Testament word means “and yet” or “although.” It is a connecting word that introduces a contrast or concession: something remains true despite what has just been stated. In ordinary English, it can link two thoughts while signaling that the second thought does not follow the expected direction. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, appearing once in Acts and once in Hebrews. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to mark an unexpected contrast.

e.t: This word describes something in ruins or the act of bringing something down. Its central sense is “to ruin” or “to tear down,” whether referring to the resulting destruction or the action that causes it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Acts 15:16 and Romans 11:3. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes a ruined condition or the tearing-down action itself.

e.t: This word means “to kiss,” describing the act of giving a kiss, often as an expression of affection, welcome, grief, or personal greeting. It can be rendered “kissed,” “kissing,” or “to kiss,” depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across six verses, including accounts involving Jesus, a welcoming father, and grieving believers. Its basic meaning remains the physical act of kissing; the surrounding passage determines the emotion or purpose expressed by that act.

Cauda is a proper name referring to a place. It is not a general quality, action, or description, but the name used for a specific location in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs once, in Acts 27:16, so its meaning is limited to this geographical name rather than a broad vocabulary concept. The surrounding verse supplies the particular significance of Cauda in that passage.

This Greek word means “edge,” referring to the outer boundary or border of something. It is a noun used five times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its basic sense identifies a limit or outermost part rather than the whole object. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what edge is being mentioned in a particular passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “pavement” or “stone pavement,” referring to a paved surface. It names a physical place or flooring made with stones rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at John 19:13. Its basic meaning is straightforward, while the precise significance of that location in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Mnason is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, and its English rendering remains “Mnason.” The name appears in Acts 21:16. Since the available word-level information identifies the person’s name but does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name itself can be explained clearly, while the person’s particular role must be understood from that passage.

This word means “to manage”—to take responsibility for organizing or administering something. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its basic sense is the handling of matters placed under someone’s care. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Luke 16:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains responsible management. e.t: This word means “at all” or “completely,” adding force to a statement. It can emphasize that something is true without exception or carried out in full. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing once in Matthew and three times in 1 Corinthians. Its exact emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears, but its normal function is to strengthen the extent or completeness of what is being said.

e.t: This word means “not yet,” indicating that something has not happened or is not true up to the present point being discussed. It combines negation with a sense of time, so it can describe an unfinished event, an unrealized condition, or something still awaited. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times, showing a recurring way to mark that a situation has not reached its expected or stated point. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what action or condition is being said to remain incomplete.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to break” or “to transgress.” It describes crossing a line of what is required or permitted, so it can refer to violating an instruction or obligation. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, twice in Matthew and once in Acts. Its basic sense centers on departing from an established requirement rather than simply making a mistake. The surrounding verse determines what particular command, duty, or boundary is involved.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “be a stranger” or “to live as a stranger.” It describes someone residing in a place without belonging to it as a native, emphasizing the condition of living as an outsider or temporary resident. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Hebrews. Its basic sense concerns a person’s status as a foreigner or resident away from the place regarded as home, rather than simply describing someone unfamiliar to others.

e.t: This word means “wide,” describing something that extends broadly from side to side. It can refer to a broad physical space, such as a way or road, rather than something narrow or confined. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 10 times in 10 verses, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding noun or description determines exactly what is wide. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation and functions as a descriptive word expressing breadth or spaciousness.

Foreknowledge means knowing something beforehand. The word refers to prior knowledge or awareness, focusing on what is known before an event or action occurs. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice: in Acts 2:23 and 1 Peter 1:2. Both occurrences are rendered “foreknowledge,” supporting this straightforward sense. The word itself identifies knowledge that precedes what follows; the surrounding verse determines how that idea functions in each passage.

e.t: This word means “to expend” or “to spend lavishly,” describing the act of using something up or spending it freely. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:43. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea is lavish or complete expenditure.

e.t: This word means “to talk to” or “to talk with,” describing direct conversation with another person. It focuses on addressing or speaking to someone rather than merely mentioning them. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts. The surrounding context determines who is being addressed and what is said, but the word itself centers on personal communication.

This word refers to a trumpeter—someone who plays a trumpet. Its glosses are “trumpeter” and “trumpeters,” identifying a person by this musical role rather than naming the instrument itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Revelation 18:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the word’s basic meaning can be stated clearly, while its particular force in that passage belongs to its context.

This word refers to a person’s family or kindred—the relatives connected to someone by family ties. It describes one’s wider family group rather than an isolated individual. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each time referring to family relationships. Its uses appear once in Luke and twice in Acts, and the consistent rendering “kindred” supports the sense of relatives or family members. The precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a “debater” or “philosopher”—a person associated with argument, discussion, or philosophical reasoning. It identifies someone recognized for engaging in learned debate rather than describing an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 1:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to a person known for intellectual argument or philosophical thought.

e.t: This word describes coming together, especially to “assemble” or “eat with” others. It can point either to gathering people in one place or to joining them at a meal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:4, so its broader range must be understood from these basic meanings rather than from repeated uses. The word presents shared presence and fellowship as an action involving more than one person.

The word means perfection: it points to completeness or a state of being fully complete. It describes the quality of lacking nothing necessary for completeness, rather than an incomplete condition. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, once in Colossians and once in Hebrews. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but the central idea remains perfection—complete fullness.

This word means “sound” or “voice,” referring to something heard. It can describe a sound made by speech or by an instrument, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Romans and once in 1 Corinthians. Its basic sense concerns an audible expression or noise, while the surrounding words determine whether the focus is a spoken voice, a musical sound, or another heard signal.

e.t: This word means “to guard,” describing the action of watching over or protecting someone or something. It can refer to active custody, keeping something secure, or preventing harm. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages associated with guarding people or preserving them. Its exact force—whether physical protection or watchful keeping—depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains protection under careful watch.

This word means “encompass” or “to surround,” describing the action of forming a boundary around something or someone. In its one occurrence in the Greek New Testament, it refers to being surrounded rather than merely approached or nearby. The word therefore conveys complete encircling: those within are enclosed by those around them. Its precise force in Revelation 20:9 depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning is the act of surrounding or encompassing.
